opus-5.5.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you mean by "useful." If you mean a robot that can reliably do one or two well-defined tasks in a fairly controlled home, like loading a dishwasher or folding laundry, we're getting surprisingly close. The progress in the last couple of years, especially from combining large pretrained models with lots of teleoperated demonstration data, has been really striking. You can now see demos of robots doing long, multi-step manipulation tasks that would have seemed like science fiction not long ago.

But there's a big gap between a demo and a product you'd actually trust in your home every day. The hard part isn't doing a task once; it's doing it the thousandth time, in a kitchen the robot has never seen, with a cup that's a slightly different shape, a kid's toy on the floor, and the lighting changed. Robustness and generalization are still the core bottlenecks. In language models, a 95% success rate is amazing. In a household robot, a 5% failure rate means broken dishes, or worse, safety issues, every single day.

There are also practical issues people tend to underestimate: hardware cost, durability of hands and actuators, battery life, and safety around people and pets. And there's data. We don't have an internet-scale dataset of physical interaction the way we do for text, so a lot of effort is going into figuring out how to collect or simulate that data efficiently.

So my honest guess: within the next few years, we'll see humanoid or mobile manipulator robots doing narrow, useful chores in early-adopter homes and in semi-structured settings like warehouses and hotels. A genuinely general-purpose household helper that you can just hand any chore to, at a price a normal family can afford, I'd say that's more like a five to ten year horizon, and probably arriving gradually rather than in one breakthrough moment.

r001.rationale: It predicts narrow, useful chores in early-adopter homes within the next few years.

r002.rationale: It describes robustness and generalization as bottlenecks, but does not say usable humanoid hardware is further along than the models and control algorithms.

r003.rationale: It gives a five-to-ten-year horizon for a genuinely general-purpose household helper.

r004.rationale: It places early robots in semi-structured settings and limits them to narrow chores, indicating relatively constrained operating scenarios.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, closer than most people think on the hardware side, and further than the demos suggest on the intelligence side.

If you look at the humanoids coming out of companies in China and the US right now, the body is largely solved. The actuators, the hands with enough degrees of freedom, the battery life to run for a couple of hours — that's all engineering, and engineering gets cheaper every year. Five years ago a humanoid cost as much as a house. Now you can buy one for the price of a car, and in a few years it'll be the price of a scooter.

The hard part is the brain. A kitchen is one of the most chaotic environments on Earth. Every house is different, every cup is in a different place, the lighting changes, there's a cat on the counter. The robot has to generalize to situations it has never seen, and that's exactly where current models still break. They look amazing in a controlled demo and then fall apart when you move the table ten centimeters.

What's changed is that we now have a path. Large foundation models for robotics, trained on huge amounts of video and teleoperation data, are starting to show the same kind of scaling behavior we saw in language. So my honest answer: a robot that can fold laundry, load a dishwasher, and tidy a room reliably in your home, not a lab — I'd say five to eight years for early adopters who are willing to tolerate mistakes, and probably ten-plus before it's as boring and dependable as a washing machine. The timeline is mostly about data. Whoever collects the most real-world household data fastest wins.

r001.rationale: The candidate estimates five to eight years for early adopters, not three to five years.

r002.rationale: It says the humanoid body is largely solved while the brain is the hard part, with current models still failing in varied homes.

r003.rationale: The five-to-eight-year estimate applies to a robot doing several named chores, and ten-plus years to washing-machine-level dependability; it does not clearly estimate five to ten years for a broad repertoire.

r004.rationale: It describes controlled demos as fragile, but does not predict that robots appearing in the first three to five years will operate in relatively fixed scenarios.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by useful household chores. If you mean a robot that can do one specific task in a fairly controlled environment, we're much closer. If you mean a robot you can bring into any home and say, “Clean up the kitchen,” and trust it to handle everything, that's still a much harder problem.

The challenge is reliability. Picking up a cup once is one thing. Handling a fragile glass, a wet plate, or something unfamiliar, with kids and pets moving around—that's a different level. And when something goes wrong, the robot needs to recover safely without you constantly helping it.

So I expect we'll see limited, useful chores first, with broader capability coming gradually. I'm optimistic, but I wouldn't put a precise date on the robot that can do everything around your house.

r001.rationale: The candidate gives no three-to-five-year prediction for a human-sized robot doing some useful chores; it says only that limited chores will come first.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability and recovery as challenges but does not say usable humanoid hardware is further along than the models or control algorithms.

r003.rationale: It gives no five-to-ten-year estimate for a robot with a broad repertoire of household tasks.

r004.rationale: It contrasts a specific task in a controlled environment with broad household capability, but does not predict that early household robots will appear within three to five years or describe them as operating in fixed scenarios.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by useful household chores. If you mean one specific task in a home that’s been set up for the robot, we’re much closer. If you mean a robot you can bring into any home and say, “Clean the kitchen, do the laundry, and put everything away,” that’s still a very hard problem.

The challenge is reliability. Doing something correctly once is a demo. Doing it every day, around kids and pets, without breaking anything or needing someone to rescue it—that’s a product. And homes have so much variation: different objects, different layouts, things left in unexpected places.

So I’d expect gradual progress, with robots taking on a few chores first. I’m optimistic, but I’d be cautious about putting a precise date on the general-purpose household robot.

r001.rationale: The response gives no three-to-five-year prediction and says it would be cautious about naming a precise date.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability and variation in homes but does not compare the progress of humanoid hardware with models or control algorithms.

r003.rationale: The response does not estimate five to ten years for a broad-repertoire household robot.

r004.rationale: It says a robot would be closer to doing a specific task in a set-up home, but does not predict that robots arriving in the first three to five years will operate in fixed scenarios.
